cards.front: A line from the centre to the circumference is a [ ___ ].
cards.back: A line from the centre to the circumference is a radius.

options.explanation: A radius is a line segment joining the centre of a circle to any point on its circumference.
A diameter passes through the centre and joins two points on the circumference. A segment from the centre to the circumference is a radius.
A chord joins two points on the circumference and does not have to pass through the centre. The required line segment is a radius.
A tangent touches the circumference at exactly one point but does not join that point to the centre. The correct term is radius.

cards.front: A straight line joining two points on the circumference is a [ ___ ].
cards.back: A straight line joining two points on the circumference is a chord.

options.explanation: A chord is a straight line segment whose two endpoints lie on the circumference of a circle.
An arc is a curved section of the circumference, not a straight line segment. A straight segment joining two circumference points is a chord.
A radius joins the centre to one point on the circumference. A straight segment joining two points on the circumference is a chord.
A tangent touches the circle at only one point. A straight segment with both endpoints on the circumference is called a chord.

cards.front: Why is triangle AOB isosceles when A and B lie on a circle centred at O?
cards.back: OA and OB are equal radii.

options.text: OA and OB are equal radii.
options.explanation: OA and OB both run from the centre O to the circumference, so they are radii of the same circle and therefore have equal lengths.

options.text: OA and OB are equal chords.
options.explanation: A chord has both endpoints on the circumference, whereas OA and OB each have one endpoint at the centre. They are equal radii, making the triangle isosceles.

options.text: OA and OB are parallel sides.
options.explanation: OA and OB meet at O, so they cannot be parallel. The triangle is isosceles because OA and OB are radii of the same circle and are equal.

options.text: OA and OB are equal tangents.
options.explanation: OA and OB extend from the centre to the circumference, so they are not tangents. They are equal radii, which gives the triangle two equal sides.

cards.front: A [ ___ ] touches a circle at exactly one point.
cards.back: A tangent touches a circle at exactly one point.

options.explanation: A tangent is a straight line that meets, or touches, a circle at exactly one point.
A secant crosses the circle and meets its circumference at two points. A line touching the circle at exactly one point is a tangent.
A chord is a line segment with both endpoints on the circumference, so it meets the circle at two points. The correct term is tangent.
A diameter joins two points on the circumference and passes through the centre. A line meeting the circle at exactly one point is a tangent.

cards.front: A radius meets a tangent at its point of contact. What angle is formed?

options.explanation: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius drawn to its point of contact, so the angle between them is 90°.
Confusing the diagram with an isosceles right triangle can suggest 45°. The tangent and radius are perpendicular at the point of contact, giving 90°.
An angle of 180° would place both lines along one straight line. A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the contact point, so the angle is 90°.
A 60° angle may be associated with equilateral triangles, but that fact does not apply here. The tangent-radius theorem gives an angle of 90°.

cards.front: The tangent-radius right angle is between the tangent and the [ ___ ].
cards.back: The tangent-radius right angle is between the tangent and the radius to the point of contact.

options.text: radius to the point of contact
options.explanation: The tangent is perpendicular specifically to the radius drawn from the centre to the point where the tangent touches the circle.
The perpendicular relationship does not apply to an arbitrary radius. It applies specifically to the radius drawn to the tangent’s point of contact.

options.text: chord through the point of contact
options.explanation: A chord through the contact point is not necessarily perpendicular to the tangent. The guaranteed right angle is with the radius to the point of contact.
Two tangents are not generally perpendicular to each other. The tangent-radius theorem concerns the radius drawn to the point where the tangent touches the circle.

cards.front: OA = 5 cm. AC is a 12 cm tangent at A. O, B and C are in a straight line, with B on the circle. Find BC.

options.explanation: OA is perpendicular to tangent AC, so triangle OAC is right-angled. Pythagoras gives $OC=\sqrt{5^2+12^2}=13$, then $BC=OC-OB=13-5=8$ cm.
This finds $OC$ using the 5-12-13 right triangle but forgets that BC is only the part outside the circle. Subtracting $OB=5$ gives $BC=8$ cm.
This subtracts $OA$ directly from tangent length $AC$, although those perpendicular sides cannot be combined that way. Pythagoras gives $OC=13$, so $BC=13-5=8$ cm.
This adds the radius to the tangent length, treating perpendicular lengths as though they lie on one line. Pythagoras gives $OC=13$, then $BC=13-5=8$ cm.

cards.front: If AB and AC are tangents from the same external point A, how do AB and AC compare?

options.explanation: Tangents drawn from the same external point to a circle have equal lengths, so $AB=AC$.
AB and AC share the endpoint A, so distinct segments cannot be parallel. The tangent theorem states that tangents from the same external point have equal lengths.
Each tangent is perpendicular to its own radius at its contact point, not necessarily to the other tangent. Tangents from A have equal lengths, so $AB=AC$.

options.text: AB and AC are in the ratio 2:1.
options.explanation: There is no 2:1 relationship between tangents from a common external point. The tangent-length theorem shows that their lengths are equal, giving a ratio of 1:1.

cards.front: AB and AC are tangents to a circle centred at O, touching at B and C. If ∠BAC = 40°, find ∠BOC.

options.explanation: Radii OB and OC are perpendicular to the tangents, so quadrilateral ABOC has two 90° angles. Therefore ∠BOC = 360° - 90° - 90° - 40° = 140°.
Doubling 40° incorrectly applies the centre-angle theorem to the angle between two tangents. The tangent radii form two right angles, giving ∠BOC = 180° - 40° = 140°.
The angle at the centre is not equal to the angle between the tangents. Since OB and OC are perpendicular to the tangents, ∠BOC = 180° - 40° = 140°.
Subtracting 40° directly from 360° ignores the two right angles formed by the radii and tangents. The required central angle is 180° - 40° = 140°.

cards.front: If a centre angle and circumference angle stand on the same chord or arc, how are they related?
cards.back: The centre angle is twice the circumference angle.

options.text: The centre angle is twice the circumference angle.
options.explanation: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference when both angles are subtended by the same chord or arc.

options.text: The centre angle is equal to the circumference angle.
options.explanation: Equal angles occur in the same segment, not when comparing centre and circumference angles. On the same chord or arc, the centre angle is twice the circumference angle.

options.text: The centre angle is half the circumference angle.
options.explanation: This reverses the circle theorem. The circumference angle is half the centre angle, so the centre angle is twice the circumference angle.

options.text: The centre angle is three times the circumference angle.
options.explanation: The multiplier is not three. For angles standing on the same chord or arc, the standard circle theorem states that the centre angle is twice the circumference angle.

cards.front: ∠BOC = 66° at the centre. ∠BAC stands on the same chord BC at the circumference. Find ∠BAC.

options.explanation: The angle at the circumference is half the angle at the centre when both stand on the same chord. Therefore ∠BAC = 66° ÷ 2 = 33°.
This treats the centre and circumference angles as equal. The circumference angle is half the 66° centre angle, so ∠BAC = 33°.
Multiplying 66° by two reverses the theorem. The centre angle is twice the circumference angle, so ∠BAC is 66° ÷ 2 = 33°.
Subtracting the centre angle from 180° gives an unrelated supplementary angle. The matching circumference angle is half the centre angle, so ∠BAC = 33°.

cards.front: A circumference angle is 118°. Its matching centre angle is reflex. Find the smaller centre angle.

options.explanation: The reflex centre angle is twice the 118° circumference angle, giving 236°. The smaller centre angle is therefore 360° - 236° = 124°.
Doubling 118° correctly gives the reflex centre angle, but the question asks for the smaller centre angle. Subtracting 236° from 360° gives 124°.
Halving 118° reverses the relationship and does not account for the reflex centre angle. The reflex angle is 236°, so the smaller centre angle is 124°.
Subtracting 118° from 360° incorrectly treats the circumference angle as the reflex centre angle. First double 118° to get 236°, leaving a smaller centre angle of 124°.

cards.front: A segment is the part of a circle cut off by a [ ___ ].
cards.back: A segment is the part of a circle cut off by a chord.

options.explanation: A chord is a straight line segment joining two points on a circle’s circumference. It divides the circle into two regions, each called a segment.
A radius joins the centre to the circumference and does not cut off a segment by itself. A segment is the region of a circle cut off by a chord.
A diameter is a special chord through the centre, but the general boundary that cuts off a segment is called a chord. A diameter specifically creates two semicircles.
A tangent touches the circle at exactly one point and does not cut off part of its interior. A chord joins two circumference points and cuts off a segment.

cards.front: Two angles stand on the same chord and are on the same side of that chord. What can you conclude?

options.explanation: Angles subtended by the same chord in the same segment are equal. Being on the same side of the chord ensures both vertices lie in the same segment.
Supplementary angles arise as opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral, not as angles in the same segment. Angles on the same chord and side are equal.
There is no rule requiring these angles to total 90°. The same-segment theorem states that angles subtended by the same chord on the same side are equal.
Perpendicular describes lines meeting at 90°, not a relationship between two angle sizes here. Angles standing on the same chord in the same segment are equal.

cards.front: A quadrilateral is cyclic when all four vertices lie on the [ ___ ].
cards.back: A quadrilateral is cyclic when all four vertices lie on the circumference.

options.explanation: A cyclic quadrilateral has all four vertices on the circumference of one circle. Its opposite angles consequently add to 180°.
The vertices do not all need to lie on a diameter, which is only one chord through the centre. A quadrilateral is cyclic when all vertices lie on the circumference.
A radius is a line segment from the centre to the circumference, so four vertices cannot define cyclicity by lying on it. They must lie on the circumference.
A quadrilateral cannot have all four distinct vertices at the circle’s centre. The defining condition is that all four vertices lie on the circumference.

cards.front: In a cyclic quadrilateral, what do opposite angles add to?

options.explanation: Opposite angles in any cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary, so each opposite pair has a total of 180°.
A total of 90° describes complementary angles, not opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral. Opposite angles are supplementary and therefore add to 180°.
All four interior angles of any quadrilateral total 360°, but the question asks about one pair of opposite angles. In a cyclic quadrilateral, that pair totals 180°.
This can result from subtracting a right angle from the quadrilateral’s 360° total, but it is not the cyclic rule. Opposite angles add to 180°.

cards.front: In cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, ∠ADC = 83°. Find ∠ABC.

options.explanation: Opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral add to 180°. Therefore, ∠ABC = 180° - 83° = 97°.
This assumes opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral are equal. They are supplementary, so ∠ABC = 180° - 83° = 97°.
This results from subtracting 83° from 190° rather than 180°. Opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral total 180°, giving ∠ABC = 97°.
This comes from subtracting 83° from 90°, as if the angles were complementary. Opposite cyclic-quadrilateral angles are supplementary, so ∠ABC = 97°.

cards.front: A tangent makes an angle with a chord. Which circle angle is equal to it?
cards.back: The angle in the opposite segment.

options.text: The angle in the opposite segment.
options.explanation: The alternate segment theorem states that the angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle subtended by that chord in the opposite segment.

options.text: The angle in the same segment.
options.explanation: Angles in the same segment are equal to each other, but that is a different theorem. A tangent-chord angle equals the angle in the opposite segment.

options.text: The angle at the centre of the circle.
options.explanation: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference subtended by the same arc. The tangent-chord angle instead equals the angle in the opposite segment.

options.text: The angle in the nearest semicircle.
options.explanation: An angle in a semicircle is 90°, but it is not generally equal to a tangent-chord angle. The equal angle lies in the opposite segment.

cards.front: A, B and C lie on a circle. A tangent touches at C. If ∠ABC = 61° and ∠ACB = 73°, find the angle between the tangent at C and chord CB.

options.explanation: The third angle of triangle ABC is ∠CAB = 180° - 61° - 73° = 46°. By the alternate segment theorem, this equals the tangent-chord angle.
The 61° angle is subtended by chord AC, not chord CB. Chord CB subtends ∠CAB = 46°, which equals the required tangent-chord angle.
The 73° angle is at the point of contact and is not the opposite-segment angle for chord CB. The required angle equals ∠CAB = 46°.
This is the supplement of 61°, but the tangent-chord theorem does not require that supplement. The opposite-segment angle is ∠CAB = 46°.

cards.front: If chords AB and CD intersect at E, then [ ___ ].
cards.back: If chords AB and CD intersect at E, then AE × BE = CE × DE.

options.explanation: For two chords intersecting inside a circle, the products of the two segment lengths on each chord are equal: AE × BE = CE × DE.
This incorrectly multiplies segments from different chords. The intersecting chords theorem multiplies the two parts of each complete chord, giving AE × BE = CE × DE.
This pairs diagonal segments rather than the two segments belonging to each chord. The correct relationship is AE × BE = CE × DE.
Intersecting chords do not generally have equal total lengths. Their segment products are equal, so the correct relationship is AE × BE = CE × DE.

cards.front: Chords AB and CD intersect at E. AE = 5 cm, BE = 9 cm, CE = 6 cm and DE = x. Find x.

options.explanation: The intersecting chords theorem gives 5 × 9 = 6 × x. Dividing 45 by 6 gives x = 7.5 cm.
This comes from treating the segment lengths as a direct proportion, 5/9 = 6/x. Intersecting chords require equal products, so 5 × 9 = 6x and x = 7.5 cm.
This equates the total chord lengths, using 5 + 9 = 6 + x. Chord lengths need not be equal; their segment products are, giving x = 7.5 cm.
This uses 6 × 5 ÷ 9, pairing and dividing the wrong segment lengths. The correct equation is 5 × 9 = 6x, so x = 7.5 cm.

cards.front: For two secants from the same external point, which product is equal for each secant?
cards.back: External part × whole length from the external point.

options.text: External part × whole length from the external point.
options.explanation: For two secants drawn from one external point, each secant’s external segment multiplied by its entire length from that point gives the same product.

options.text: External part × internal part inside the circle.
options.explanation: Using only the internal section omits part of the required secant length. The equal product is external part × whole length from the external point.

options.text: Whole length × whole length from the external point.
options.explanation: The whole secant length is not squared or multiplied by itself. Each product uses the external part once and the whole length once.

options.text: External part + whole length from the external point.
options.explanation: The secant theorem equates products, not sums. For each secant, multiply its external part by its whole length measured from the external point.

cards.front: From E, one secant has CE = 4 cm and CA = x. Another has DE = 3 cm and DB = 10 cm. Find x.

options.explanation: The whole lengths are 4 + x and 3 + 10 = 13. Thus 4(4 + x) = 3 × 13, giving x = 5.75 cm.
This uses external part × internal part, producing 4x = 3 × 10. The theorem requires whole lengths, so 4(4 + x) = 3 × 13 and x = 5.75 cm.
This treats DB = 10 cm as the whole second secant, using 4(4 + x) = 3 × 10. Its whole length is 13 cm, giving x = 5.75 cm.
This treats x as the whole first secant length rather than its internal part, leading to 4x = 39. The whole first secant is 4 + x, so x = 5.75 cm.
